label: Real run on this Mac's Docker Compose stack, with synthetic traffic from klaxon.traffic: synthetic data, a simulated provider, no real money. One fault from klaxon.faults, pool-exhaustion, was injected on purpose. The alert was raised by klaxon.alerts from what the stack showed. Klaxon's loop ran live on it, through Claude Code on Aravind's seat, and stopped on diagnosed after 8 steps; any reply it got is a recorded response, not a simulation. It was offered one write action (rollback_deploy), as in week 4; in an evaluation run its gate only plans an action the diagnosis names: nobody is asked, and nothing runs. The diagnosis was compared with the fault's recorded cause by a rule (klaxon.grading), not by a person or a model. Code planned the action its diagnosis named (redeploy payments-api: PROVIDER_BREAKER on (unchanged), CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT cents (unchanged), REFUND_CONNECTION kept -> returned); in an evaluation run nobody is asked, and nothing ran. The fault's cause was removed by the harness's clearing (klaxon.faults).

case.name: pool-exhaustion
case.title: Payments fail: the payments API's database pool runs dry
case.right_answer: The fault's recorded cause: a deploy of the payments API with a connection leak (REFUND_CONNECTION=kept): reading a payment's refunds takes a connection from its database pool of 10 and never gives it back, so after about ten refunds the pool is empty, and every request waits for a connection until the pool's 5 s timeout, then fails with a 500.
case.remedy: roll the payments API back to REFUND_CONNECTION=returned: its new container starts with a full pool

rerun_command: python -m klaxon.evaluation run --model claude-opus-5-5 --cases pool-exhaustion --seeds 9 --steps 10 --tool-calls 8 --rate 3 --loop langgraph

fault.name: pool-exhaustion
fault.title: Payments fail: the payments API's database pool runs dry
fault.cause: a deploy of the payments API with a connection leak (REFUND_CONNECTION=kept): reading a payment's refunds takes a connection from its database pool of 10 and never gives it back, so after about ten refunds the pool is empty, and every request waits for a connection until the pool's 5 s timeout, then fails with a 500
expected_symptoms: the pool runs dry about 40 to 50 s after the deploy; then POST /payments takes 5 to 8 s (a worker thread, then the pool's 5 s wait) and fails with a 500: the p95 latency passes 7 s, and the 5xx share passes 70% within a minute
the payments API logs 'unhandled error' with PoolTimeout: no connection within 5 s
its health check fails too, so docker marks it unhealthy, while PostgreSQL itself is up
the traffic's clients retry and give up: many payments end with their outcome unknown, and arrivals past 64 in flight are shed
the money check passes: a payment that never got a connection was never charged, and one charged before its answer was lost is confirmed by its webhook
fault.remedy: roll the payments API back to REFUND_CONNECTION=returned: its new container starts with a full pool

diagnosis.hypothesis: payments-api was redeployed at 21:36:53 with REFUND_CONNECTION=kept. The likely effect is that each refund request keeps its Postgres connection instead of returning it to the pool. Refunds stay fast (about 15 ms) while the pool fills. About a minute after the deploy, around 21:38, the pool ran out. From then on, every request that needs a database connection, POST /payments and refunds alike, waits for the pool timeout (about 5 s) and fails with psycopg_pool.PoolTimeout, which surfaces as a 500. That produces both the 5xx ratio and the roughly 7 s p95 in the alert. The provider and Redis are healthy and fast. Still open: I could not see the previous REFUND_CONNECTION value or a pool-usage metric. The 'kept' setting as the specific leak is therefore inferred from the setting's name and the timing, not observed directly. Another change in the same deploy could be the cause, but a rollback of that deploy would cover it as well.

evidence.shows: POST /payments 500s start only at 21:38:04 (1.3/s), reach 5.35/s at 21:38:34, and 201s drop to 0.46/s. This confirms the alert.
payments-api is the only service deployed after the 21:35:26 stack start, at 21:36:53, about 1 minute before the 500s began. Its settings include REFUND_CONNECTION=kept.
All payments-api errors are psycopg_pool.PoolTimeout on POST /payments, meaning the Postgres connection pool is exhausted.
Slow POST /payments traces since 21:38:04 take 5.9–6.9 s.
A slow trace has no provider or DB spans. A Redis SET at 1.7 s is followed by about 5 s of nothing, then a Redis EVAL and a 500 with PoolTimeout. The request spent that time waiting on the pool.
Provider call p95 stays about 5 ms throughout, so the provider is not slow and is not holding connections.

arguments.query: sum by (http_route, http_request_method) (rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_sum{service_name="payments-api"}[1m])) / sum by (http_route, http_request_method) (rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{service_name="payments-api"}[1m]))

evidence.shows: Before 21:38, refund and payment routes took 14–38 ms on average. Both jumped to 4–6 s at 21:38:14, consistent with a shared pool being exhausted. Refunds were not slow beforehand, which fits connections being leaked rather than held during long work.

proposed_fix.summary: Roll payments-api back to its settings before the 21:36:53 deploy, presumably a REFUND_CONNECTION mode that returns connections to the pool. Recreating the container also frees the leaked connections. Then confirm that the POST /payments 5xx rate and latency return to baseline. Run money_check to verify that refunds and payments made during the incident match the provider.

diagnosis.blast_radius: payments-api pauses while its container is recreated, so in-flight payment and refund requests may fail. Clients should retry with idempotency keys stored in Redis. If the cause is something other than this deploy, the rollback will not stop the exhaustion. Payments that failed with 500 may need to be retried by clients. Nothing already booked is repaired.
diagnosis.rollback_plan: If the rollback makes things worse, redeploy the current payments-api settings (image sha256:6352144993c2 with PROVIDER_BREAKER=on, CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents, REFUND_CONNECTION=kept). Then investigate pool sizing and connection handling directly.
